prompt.context: Our client is a Canadian pharmaceutical company. Their first drug has just been approved by what is equivalent to the United States' FDA and is an asthma treatment. The client has hired McKinsey to help them assess what is the right price for this new treatment and they will also need McKinsey's help with completing an application to the government for price approval. Canada's government subsidizes healthcare costs and pays back its citizens for medical treatments.
prompt.question: What is the right price for this new asthma treatment drug? Specifically, determine both a minimum and maximum price the client should charge.

clarifying_info.q: What are the R&D costs for this drug?
clarifying_info.a: R&D costs are estimated to be $5 billion.

clarifying_info.q: What are the marketing and variable costs?
clarifying_info.a: For this case, assume marketing costs are $0 and there are no variable costs.

clarifying_info.q: What are the market segments and their usage patterns?
clarifying_info.a: There are three segments: Basic (2% of population, periodic asthma attacks, 1 inhaler/month), Serious (2% of population, 1 inhaler/week), Acute (1% of population, 1 inhaler/week, but attacks sometimes result in hospitalization and death).

clarifying_info.q: How does the new treatment work / what form does it take?
clarifying_info.a: The treatment is classified as preventative. It is a pill that must be taken every day.

clarifying_info.q: How much do current inhalers cost?
clarifying_info.a: Regular inhalers cost $10 each. This is the common treatment for asthma.

clarifying_info.q: What are the hospitalization costs for acute patients?
clarifying_info.a: Acute patients that result in hospitalization spend 1 night/year in the hospital at $1,000 and the rate of death is 1%.

framework: Cost-based pricing: set price at cost plus markup (break-even minimum)
Value-based pricing: set price at what customers (and government) are willing to pay (maximum)
Determine minimum price via break-even analysis on R&D costs over 5 years
Determine maximum price via government's current total spend on inhalers and hospitalizations
Compare minimum and maximum to arrive at recommended price range

questions.prompt: Using cost-based pricing, calculate the break-even price per pill (minimum price).
questions.guidance: Candidate should size the Canadian asthma market (30M population x 5% asthmatic = 1.5M people), set break-even revenue over 5 years equal to $5B R&D, compute revenue per patient, then divide by number of pills per patient over 5 years (350 days/year x 5 years = 1,750 pills).

math.setup: Total asthma patients = 30M x 5% = 1.5M. Break-even: 1.5M x revenue per person = $5B. Revenue per person = $5B / 1.5M = ~$3,333. Pills over 5 years = 350 days/year x 5 years = 1,750. Price per pill = $3,333 / 1,750.
steps: Pills per patient over 5 years = 350 x 5 = 1,750

questions.prompt: Calculate the government's current annual and 5-year total spend on inhalers across all three segments.
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate annual inhaler cost per person per segment, multiply by segment population, sum across segments. Basic: $10/inhaler x 12 inhalers/year = $120/year. Serious and Acute: $10/inhaler x 52 inhalers/year = $520/year.

math.setup: Canada population = 30M. Basic = 2% x 30M = 600,000 people, 1 inhaler/month = 12/year at $10 = $120/year. Serious = 2% x 30M = 600,000 people, 1 inhaler/week = 52/year at $10 = $520/year. Acute = 1% x 30M = 300,000 people, 1 inhaler/week = 52/year at $10 = $520/year.

questions.prompt: Calculate the government's additional current annual spend on acute patient hospitalizations.
questions.guidance: Only acute patients are hospitalized. 300,000 acute patients x 1 night/year x $1,000/night.

math.setup: Acute patients = 300,000. Hospitalization rate = 1 night/year at $1,000 per night.

questions.prompt: Calculate the government's total current spend over 5 years and use this to determine the maximum price.
questions.guidance: Total annual government spend = inhaler spend + hospitalization spend. Multiply by 5 years to get 5-year total. This 5-year total is the maximum the government would pay for the new drug (since it would otherwise pay this amount under the current treatment regime). Candidate should note that the minimum ($5B R&D break-even) exceeds the 5-year government spend ($4.2B), indicating a pricing challenge.

math.answer: $4.2 billion over 5 years (maximum the government would subsidize based on current spend)

brainstorming.prompt: Summarize the minimum and maximum price range. What other factors or parameters should be considered when recommending a final price?

categories.name: Pricing range summary
ideas: Minimum price: ~$2/pill (break-even on $5B R&D over 5 years for 1.5M patients)
Maximum price: equivalent to $4.2B total government current spend over 5 years, roughly $2.80/pill ($4.2B / 1.5M patients / 1,750 pills)
The minimum ($5B break-even) exceeds the 5-year government budget ($4.2B), suggesting a tension in pricing

categories.name: Drug patent considerations
ideas: Patent life determines the window to recover R&D costs
After patent expiry, generic competition will compress price

categories.name: Market expansion
ideas: International market potential beyond Canada could spread R&D costs over a larger base
Pricing in Canada need not fully cover all R&D if other markets also pay
Larger global market reduces the per-unit minimum price needed to break even

categories.name: Value considerations
ideas: Preventative treatment vs. symptomatic treatment — preventative drugs may command a premium for improved quality of life
Reduction in hospitalizations and deaths for acute patients provides additional value beyond inhaler cost savings
Government may value mortality reduction (1% death rate in acute patients) as justifying a higher price

categories.name: Barriers to adoption
ideas: Not all current inhaler users will switch — some patients may prefer inhalers
Patient compliance with daily pill regimen may be lower than assumed
Physicians and pharmacists may resist switching established patients

recommendation: The minimum price is approximately $2/pill, based on break-even of $5B R&D over 5 years across 1.5M Canadian asthmatic patients taking the pill daily

The maximum price the Canadian government would subsidize is approximately equivalent to its current 5-year total spend of $4.2B on inhalers and hospitalizations — roughly $2.80/pill assuming full market adoption

The company faces a pricing gap: the break-even cost ($5B over 5 years) exceeds the government's current total spend ($4.2B), so either the payback horizon must be extended beyond 5 years, or international markets must be factored in to cover the remaining R&D
risks: If adoption is less than 100% of the 1.5M asthma population, the per-patient cost burden increases and break-even price rises
Government may not agree to subsidize a drug whose total cost exceeds current treatment spend
Competitive drugs or off-patent generics could enter the market and erode price
next_steps: Model scenarios with longer payback periods (e.g., 7-10 years) to find a price that both covers R&D and stays within government subsidy limits
Assess international market size to determine how much R&D cost can be allocated outside Canada
Prepare the government application highlighting the preventative value, quality-of-life improvement, and long-term hospitalization/death reduction savings
